title: Three.js performance — 39 tips across monitoring, scene, assets, renderer and shaders
body: > Compiled from course notes and the performance chapter of [Three.js Journey](https://threejs-journey.com/), with reference to [discoverthreejs.com](https://discoverthreejs.com/tips-and-tricks/). The original notes targeted an older three.js; several APIs have changed since, and the corrections are listed at the end. Target **60fps**. Gamers may expect more. There are only two limits: the **CPU** and the **GPU**. Two prerequisites: 1. **Do the ordinary frontend optimizations before touching 3D.** DNS prefetching, lazy loading, asset compression — that is the foundation, and 3D work on a bad foundation is wasted. (3D projects usually need neither SSR nor SSG.) 2. **Test on real devices**, especially mobile. Your M-series Mac running smoothly says nothing about your users. --- ## 1. Monitoring ### 1 — Monitor FPS Use three.js's own `stats.js`, wrapping the whole frame in `tick`: ```js const tick = () => { stats.begin(); // ... stats.end(); }; ``` DevTools also works: **More tools → Rendering → Frame rendering stats**. ### 2 — Unlock the frame rate limit Chrome caps rendering at the display refresh rate. Without unlocking it, a steady 60fps on a good machine is misleading — the site may only reach 70fps there and drop below 60 elsewhere. Unlocked, you should see 150–200fps on a strong machine to feel safe. > Unlocking is done via launch flags, **but it can crash the browser — use it only for local profiling.** ### 3 — Monitor draw calls A draw call is the GPU drawing triangles. More objects, geometries and materials means more draw calls. **Fewer is better.** Use the **Spector.js** Chrome extension (built by the Babylon.js team, but coupled to neither Babylon nor three.js): click the icon to activate, click the red circle to record a frame, then read the **Commands** tab. Blue steps are draw calls; the rest is data sent to the GPU — matrices, attributes, uniforms. **Note: Spector.js only works with WebGL, not WebGPU.** ### 4 — Renderer information The cheapest check there is: ```js console.log(renderer.info); ``` You get geometry and texture counts plus this frame's draw calls and triangles. --- ## 2. General ### 5 — Performant JavaScript `tick` runs every frame, so the code inside it directly determines frame rate. Keep ESLint on it; avoid allocations and `new` in there. In react-three-fiber there is no `tick` — the equivalent is the `useFrame` hook. ### 6 — Dispose of things Free resources as soon as you are sure you no longer need them. In a level-based game, dispose of the previous level on transition: ```js scene.remove(cube); cube.geometry.dispose(); cube.material.dispose(); ``` --- ## 3. Lights ### 7 — Avoid them Lights are simple to use and **steadily drain performance** — materials that support lighting are expensive to compute. Five or six lights in one scene is a disaster. If you must, pick the cheap ones: `AmbientLight`, `DirectionalLight`. **Emissive materials** can sometimes stand in for a light at a fraction of the cost. ### 8 — Avoid adding or removing lights Adding or removing a light forces **every light-supporting material to recompile**. In a complex scene that freezes the frame. Once the scene is set up, leave the lights alone. --- ## 4. Shadows ### 9 — Avoid them Same reasoning as lights. Prefer alternatives — **baked shadows**, where the shadow is painted into the texture, look better and cost nothing in a static scene. ### 10 — Optimize shadow maps Use `CameraHelper` to see what the shadow camera actually renders, then shrink it to the minimum: ```js directionalLight.shadow.camera.top = 3; directionalLight.shadow.camera.right = 6; directionalLight.shadow.camera.left = -6; directionalLight.shadow.camera.bottom = -3; directionalLight.shadow.camera.far = 10; scene.add(new THREE.CameraHelper(directionalLight.shadow.camera)); ``` Drop the resolution as far as the result allows: ```js directionalLight.shadow.mapSize.set(1024, 1024); ``` ### 11 — Use castShadow and receiveShadow deliberately Some objects only cast, some only receive, few need both. **Enable each on as few objects as possible:** ```js cube.castShadow = true; cube.receiveShadow = false; floor.castShadow = false; floor.receiveShadow = true; ``` ### 12 — Deactivate shadow auto-update By default the shadow map is recomputed before every render. A static scene does not need that: ```js renderer.shadowMap.autoUpdate = false; renderer.shadowMap.needsUpdate = true; // trigger manually when needed ``` The rule is simple: **if the object does not move, its shadow does not need to either.** --- ## 5. Textures ### 13 — Resize textures Textures take a lot of GPU memory, and mipmaps make it worse. **Resolution is what matters, not file size** — a 100KB 4096×4096 JPEG costs the same in VRAM as a 5MB PNG of the same dimensions. Reduce resolution as far as the visual result permits. ### 14 — Keep power-of-two resolutions This matters for mipmaps. It need not be square — width and height can differ — but both should be powers of two. Otherwise three.js resizes to the nearest power of two, which costs resources and can degrade quality. ### 15 — Use the right format - Run jpg/png through TinyPNG or similar - **Prefer KTX2** (`.ktx2`, Khronos's supercompressed GPU texture format) — small files, and crucially **it stays compressed in GPU memory** Measured example: switching a texture set to KTX2 barely changed file size, but **removed the quality loss and cut GPU memory to 21.43MB**. Compared to game bundles measured in tens of gigabytes, file size matters less than VRAM. --- ## 6. Geometries ### 16 — Everything is a BufferGeometry **This is no longer something to worry about.** Before **r125**, three.js had non-buffer `Geometry` objects that stored vertices, faces and colours directly — convenient but slow, and converted to `BufferGeometry` at render time anyway. **`THREE.Geometry` was removed in r125.** All geometries are buffer geometries now. Any tutorial telling you to "use plain Geometry when there aren't many objects" predates 2021. ### 17 — Do not update vertices Updating a geometry's vertices is terrible for performance. Doing it once at creation is fine; **never do it in `tick`.** To animate vertices, use a **vertex shader**. ### 18 — Mutualize geometries When several meshes share a shape, create the geometry once: ```js const geometry = new THREE.BoxGeometry(0.5, 0.5, 0.5); const material = new THREE.MeshNormalMaterial(); for (let i = 0; i < 50; i++) { const mesh = new THREE.Mesh(geometry, material); // same geometry reused mesh.position.set( (Math.random() - 0.5) * 10, (Math.random() - 0.5) * 10, (Math.random() - 0.5) * 10 ); scene.add(mesh); } ``` ### 19 — Merge geometries If those objects never need to move independently, merge them into one geometry with one mesh — 50 draw calls become 1: ```js import * as BufferGeometryUtils from 'three/addons/utils/BufferGeometryUtils.js'; const geometries = []; for (let i = 0; i < 50; i++) { const geometry = new THREE.BoxGeometry(0.5, 0.5, 0.5); geometry.rotateX((Math.random() - 0.5) * Math.PI * 2); geometry.translate( (Math.random() - 0.5) * 10, (Math.random() - 0.5) * 10, (Math.random() - 0.5) * 10 ); geometries.push(geometry); } const merged = BufferGeometryUtils.mergeGeometries(geometries); scene.add(new THREE.Mesh(merged, new THREE.MeshNormalMaterial())); ``` ⚠️ **The API was renamed.** `mergeBufferGeometries` from older tutorials has been **removed**; it is now **`mergeGeometries`**. Copying old code gives you an undefined error. The precondition is that relative positions are fixed — after merging there is a single mesh, so individual objects can no longer be moved. Very useful in WebGIS-style scenes. --- ## 7. Materials ### 20 — Mutualize materials Same as geometries: create one material of a given kind and share it. ### 21 — Use cheap materials Roughly, from most to least expensive: ``` MeshPhysicalMaterial > MeshStandardMaterial > MeshPhongMaterial > MeshLambertMaterial > MeshBasicMaterial ``` `MeshStandardMaterial` and `MeshPhysicalMaterial` are physically based (PBR) — good looking and costly. Pick the cheapest material that gives the look you need. --- ## 8. Meshes ### 22 — Use InstancedMesh For many objects with **the same geometry and material differing only in transform** (bridge railings, a forest, a field of cubes), use `InstancedMesh` — one draw call for all instances. ```js const mesh = new THREE.InstancedMesh(geometry, material, 50); scene.add(mesh); for (let i = 0; i < 50; i++) { const position = new THREE.Vector3( (Math.random() - 0.5) * 10, (Math.random() - 0.5) * 10, (Math.random() - 0.5) * 10 ); const quaternion = new THREE.Quaternion().setFromEuler( new THREE.Euler((Math.random() - 0.5) * Math.PI * 2, (Math.random() - 0.5) * Math.PI * 2, 0) ); const matrix = new THREE.Matrix4(); matrix.makeRotationFromQuaternion(quaternion); matrix.setPosition(position); mesh.setMatrixAt(i, matrix); } ``` Nearly as good as merging geometries, **but each instance can still be transformed individually** — that is its advantage over tip 19. If you will change matrices inside `tick`, declare the usage: ```js mesh.instanceMatrix.setUsage(THREE.DynamicDrawUsage); ``` --- ## 9. Models ### 23 — Low poly Fewer polygons, better frame rate. Where detail is needed, use **normal maps** — they buy a lot of apparent geometry at texture cost, which is a very good trade. ### 24 — Draco compression Compress geometry-heavy models with Draco; the size reduction is substantial. **Three limits worth remembering:** 1. **Draco compresses geometry, not textures.** If the weight comes from large PBR textures, Draco will not help — go compress the textures instead. 2. **Decompression has a cost**: a possible freeze while decoding, plus the Draco decoder library to load. 3. **It does not combine with server-side compression.** Gzipping already-Draco data gains almost nothing and the configurations tend to interfere. The rule: **Draco pays off when there are no large PBR textures.** ### 25 — Server-side compression Gzip / Brotli, configured on the server (Nginx, Apache, Node). **Most servers do not compress `.glb` / `.gltf` / `.obj` by default** — add those MIME types explicitly. ⚠️ **Mutually exclusive with incremental loading (tip 27)** and with progress bars — see below. ### 26 — LOD Distant objects do not need full detail. Prepare a few levels and switch by distance — the same idea as ``. ```js const lod = new THREE.LOD(); lod.addLevel(highDetailMesh, 0); lod.addLevel(lowDetailMesh, 50); scene.add(lod); ``` Essential in large-world projects — GTA, PUBG, WebGIS. In the react-three-fiber ecosystem, **drei** provides `` for this. Other fallbacks: update distant animations every 2–3 frames, or replace far objects with billboards. ### 27 — Incremental loading Render part of a model while the rest is still downloading. State of support: **three.js does not support it**; Babylon.js manages via the `.incremental.babylon` format (Blender needs a plugin to export it); UE and Unity support it. Doing this with glTF requires converting to a binary stream and is considerably more work. ⚠️ **Gzip disables incremental loading**, because compressed responses cannot be fetched with HTTP Range requests. For the same reason, **a progress bar also rules out gzip** — progress is computed from `Content-Length`, which no longer reflects the original size. --- ## 10. Cameras ### 28 — Field of view Objects outside the field of view are not rendered — **frustum culling**. A narrower FOV means fewer objects on screen and fewer triangles. ### 29 — Near and far Likewise, tighten `near` and `far`. In a vast world of mountains, trees and buildings, the user cannot see the small houses behind the mountains — lower `far` and they will not even be considered. --- ## 11. Renderer ### 30 — Pixel ratio Some devices have very high pixel ratios (recent iPhones are 3:1). More pixels to render, worse frame rate. Cap it at 2 when performance suffers: ```js renderer.setPixelRatio(Math.min(window.devicePixelRatio, 2)); ``` This is a **quality/performance trade-off** — decide per project. > Related: models looking blurry on a Mac is usually an unhandled DPR issue. ### 31 — Power preference Some devices switch between GPUs (integrated vs discrete) or power modes. Hint at instantiation: ```js const renderer = new THREE.WebGLRenderer({ canvas, powerPreference: 'high-performance', }); ``` Desktop: `high-performance`. Mobile: weigh it against battery. **If you have no performance issue, use `'default'`.** ⚠️ Spelling matters. A misspelled value such as `'high-performatnce'` throws no error and **silently falls back to the default** — you think it is on, and it is not. ### 32 — Antialias The default antialiasing is reasonably fast, but **still slower than none**. Enable it only when aliasing is visible and performance allows. ### 33 — Offscreen rendering / Web Worker Move rendering into a Web Worker with `OffscreenCanvas` so the main thread is not blocked. **The environment must be headless (no DOM).** three.js and Babylon.js support this; **DOM-dependent 2D libraries such as Phaser and PixiJS do not.** The same idea applies to **physics**: the physics world and the 3D world are already separate, so running the physics engine (cannon, for instance) on its own thread is a clear win. Communicate with `postMessage` or `SharedArrayBuffer`. > Aside: with `headless-gl` and `node-canvas`, three.js and Babylon.js also run under Node — they do not strictly require a browser host. --- ## 12. Postprocessing ### 34 — Limit passes **Every postprocessing pass repaints the full screen at render resolution, pixel ratio included.** The arithmetic makes the cost obvious. At 1920×1080, pixel ratio 2, four passes: ``` 1920 × 2 × 1080 × 2 × 4 = 33,177,600 pixels ``` Group your custom passes into one where possible. --- ## 13. Shaders ### 35 — Specify the precision ```js const shaderMaterial = new THREE.ShaderMaterial({ precision: 'lowp', // ... }); ``` Check for quality loss or banding afterwards. `RawShaderMaterial` ignores this property — declare `precision` in the shader source yourself. ### 36 — Keep the code simple **Avoid `if` statements.** Make good use of swizzles and built-in functions. Use `clamp` instead of a branch: ```glsl modelPosition.y += clamp(elevation, 0.5, 1.0) * uDisplacementStrength; ``` And `mix` instead of hand-rolled colour formulas in the fragment shader: ```glsl vec3 finalColor = mix(depthColor, surfaceColor, elevation); ``` ### 37 — Use textures instead of noise functions Perlin noise is elegant but expensive. **`texture2D()` is far cheaper**, and noise textures are easy to author in tools like Photoshop. ### 38 — Use defines instead of uniforms Uniforms are convenient — tweakable and animatable from JavaScript — but they have a cost. **If the value never changes, use a define:** ```glsl #define uDisplacementStrength 1.5 ``` With `ShaderMaterial`, entries in `defines` are injected into the GLSL automatically. ### 39 — Do calculations in the vertex shader There are far fewer vertices than fragments. Anything that can be computed per-vertex and passed down should not be computed per-fragment. --- ## Appendix: two bundling notes **Three.js and Babylon.js are large, and still large after gzip.** Two mitigations: 1. **Import only what you use.** Importing Babylon.js globally costs 5MB and defeats tree-shaking. 2. **CDN + externals.** Configure it as a Webpack external and load from a CDN — assuming that CDN is reliable. If production needs shader compilation (writing WebGL shaders inside React via something like `gl-react`), Webpack's ecosystem is more complete than Vite's here. --- ## Corrections The original notes targeted an older version. The following were updated: | Original | Correction | |---|---| | `Geometry` is friendlier than `BufferGeometry` but slower; use it when object counts are low | **`THREE.Geometry` was removed in r125** — only BufferGeometry exists now | | `BufferGeometryUtils.mergeBufferGeometries()` | Renamed to **`mergeGeometries()`**; the old name is gone | | `powerPreference: 'high-performatnce'` | Typo — the correct value is `'high-performance'`; invalid values fall back silently | | "web worker render" (heading with no content) | Filled in as tip 33: `OffscreenCanvas` plus the headless requirement | | Incremental loading linked straight to the Babylon.js docs | Noted that three.js does not support it, and that it conflicts with gzip and progress bars | | Material cost section had mismatched links (Phong linking to Physical) | Replaced with an ordered cost list | | `print(renderer.info)` in a Python code block | Should be `console.log(renderer.info)` in JavaScript | --- ## Related - [The five layers of React performance work](/blog?post=73)
